label: PYQ-style
stem: Give reasons: (i) aromatic diazonium salts are more stable than aliphatic diazonium salts; (ii) the p$K_b$ of aniline is higher than that of methylamine.
model_answer:
(i) The positive charge of the arenediazonium ion is delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance; an alkyldiazonium ion has no such stabilisation. [1]
(ii) In aniline the lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring and is less available for protonation; in methylamine the +I effect of $\ce{-CH3}$ increases electron density on N. Aniline is the weaker base, so its p$K_b$ is higher. [1]

(ii) In aniline the lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring and is less available for protonation; in methylamine the +I effect of $\ce{-CH3}$ increases electron density on N. Aniline is the weaker base, so its p$K_b$ is higher.

hint: (i) Resonance with the benzene ring. (ii) Where is the lone pair of aniline spread?

label: PYQ-style
stem: Describe the Hinsberg test for distinguishing primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
model_answer:
The amine is shaken with benzenesulphonyl chloride ($\ce{C6H5SO2Cl}$, Hinsberg's reagent) in the presence of alkali.
**Primary amine:** forms N-alkylbenzenesulphonamide, which is *soluble in alkali* because the H on nitrogen is acidic. [1]
**Secondary amine:** forms N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, which has no H on nitrogen and is *insoluble in alkali*. [1]
**Tertiary amine:** does not react. [1]

**Secondary amine:** forms N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide, which has no H on nitrogen and is *insoluble in alkali*.
**Tertiary amine:** does not react.

hint: Reagent: benzenesulphonyl chloride. Watch whether the product dissolves in alkali.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Give reasons: (i) direct nitration of aniline gives a substantial amount of m-nitroaniline; (ii) aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis; (iii) $\ce{(CH3)2NH}$ is a stronger base than $\ce{(CH3)3N}$ in aqueous solution. [3]
(b) Give one chemical test each to distinguish (i) aniline and N-methylaniline, (ii) ethanamine and aniline. [2]
model_answer:
(a)(i) In the strongly acidic nitrating mixture aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion, which is meta-directing. [1]
(ii) Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion (the C–X bond has partial double-bond character). [1]
(iii) The protonated secondary amine is better stabilised by hydrogen bonding with water (two N–H) and is less crowded than the protonated tertiary amine (one N–H); this outweighs the extra +I effect in the tertiary amine. [1]
(b)(i) **Carbylamine test:** on heating with $\ce{CHCl3}$ and alcoholic KOH, aniline gives a foul-smelling isocyanide; N-methylaniline (a secondary amine) does not. [1]
(ii) **Azo dye test:** treat with $\ce{NaNO2}$ + HCl at 273–278 K, then add alkaline $\beta$-naphthol. Aniline gives an orange-red dye; ethanamine gives off $\ce{N2}$ bubbles and no dye. [1]

scheme.step: (a)(i) In the strongly acidic nitrating mixture aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion, which is meta-directing.
(ii) Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion (the C–X bond has partial double-bond character).

(iii) The protonated secondary amine is better stabilised by hydrogen bonding with water (two N–H) and is less crowded than the protonated tertiary amine (one N–H); this outweighs the extra +I effect in the tertiary amine.
(b)(i) **Carbylamine test:** on heating with $\ce{CHCl3}$ and alcoholic KOH, aniline gives a foul-smelling isocyanide; N-methylaniline (a secondary amine) does not.
(ii) **Azo dye test:** treat with $\ce{NaNO2}$ + HCl at 273–278 K, then add alkaline $\beta$-naphthol. Aniline gives an orange-red dye; ethanamine gives off $\ce{N2}$ bubbles and no dye.

hint: In strong acid aniline becomes the anilinium ion. Aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution.

stem: *Many bright orange, red and yellow dyes used on cloth are azo compounds. To make one, a primary aromatic amine such as aniline is first treated with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid in a vessel cooled with ice. The cold solution is used at once: it is added to a solution of a phenol or another aromatic amine, and the coloured dye separates out.*

parts.stem: Write the equation for the reaction of aniline with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid in the cold.

scheme.step: $\begin{gathered}\ce{C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl}\\ \ce{->[273-278 K] C6H5N2+Cl-}\\ \text{+ }\ce{NaCl + 2H2O}\end{gathered}$

parts.stem: Why must the mixture be kept in ice and the product used at once?
parts.model_answer: The diazonium salt is unstable: above about 278 K it decomposes, reacting with water to give phenol and nitrogen. [1]

scheme.step: The diazonium salt is unstable: above about 278 K it decomposes, reacting with water to give phenol and nitrogen.

parts.stem: Name the product and its colour when the cold solution is added to phenol in alkaline medium. Why are such compounds coloured?
parts.model_answer: p-Hydroxyazobenzene (4-hydroxyazobenzene), an orange dye, formed by coupling at the para position. [1] The two rings joined through –N=N– form an extended conjugated system that absorbs visible light. [1]

scheme.step: p-Hydroxyazobenzene (4-hydroxyazobenzene), an orange dye, formed by coupling at the para position.
The two rings joined through –N=N– form an extended conjugated system that absorbs visible light.

hint: The first step is diazotisation; the second is coupling. Ask what the diazonium salt does if it warms up.
